options.text: In northeastern China, a dance of the Korean community takes its steps from farming. Dancers mime walking the ridges between fields to drums, gongs and the piercing sound of a suona.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Hunan’s Wulingyuan landscape, more than 3,000 sandstone pillars and peaks rise above the ravines. Many individual pillars are taller than 200 metres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Traditional Chinese block printers prepare smooth planks of pear or jujube wood only two centimetres thick. An image starts on thin paper before an engraver cuts it into the wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Listen to vallenato from the Magdalena region and you can hear several histories at once. Cattle herders’ songs, African chants, Indigenous dance rhythms and Spanish verse all helped shape it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A varnished wooden object from Pasto begins far from the woodshop. Harvesters collect buds in the forests of Putumayo to make the material decorators call mopa-mopa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Barranquilla’s four days of carnival reflect its past as a Caribbean trading port. Dance traditions from Colombia’s interior met European and African ones there.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Cuban son, the bass helps tell the dancers where to step. Musicians improvise around patterns, drawing lyrics from everyday life and passing songs on by ear.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: After upheavals in Haiti in the 1790s, enslaved people brought tumba francesa to eastern Cuba. Its dances joined French forms with musical traditions from West Africa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The palaces in Cuba’s city of Trinidad trace the fortunes of sugar. The Brunet and Cantero mansions date from the town’s prosperity in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Ecuadorian pasillo takes its name from the dancers’ “small step.” Its music brings an Andean song tradition together with the waltz, minuet and Spanish bolero.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: About a thousand kilometres off mainland Ecuador, three ocean currents meet around the Galápagos. The islands’ unusual mix of marine life begins with that underwater crossroads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The finest Ecuadorian toquilla hats take as long as eight months to weave. Workers strip the palm fibre, boil it and dry it before weaving the crown and brim.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Egypt, Coptic Christians and Muslims take part in festivals that commemorate the Holy Family’s flight from Bethlehem. Processions retrace parts of the journey.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The pyramids of Giza belong to a much larger landscape of the dead. Around the old capital of Memphis, it stretches to Dahshur and includes rock-cut tombs and low, flat-roofed mastabas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Egypt’s Western Desert contains a valley full of early whale fossils. Wadi Al-Hitan preserves the transition from land-dwelling mammals to whales that spent their lives at sea.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some of the last surviving traditional buildings of the Asante near Kumasi are made from earth, timber and straw. Keeping them standing means caring for materials the rains readily wear away.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A lead singer calls and a chorus answers in Ghanaian highlife. Guitars and horns can share the rhythm with drums and xylophones, in songs drawn from daily life.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Ghanaian kente cloth can have a proverb for a name. Weavers make narrow strips on horizontal looms, choosing patterns and colours that can signal who will wear the fabric.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Starting in 930, people gathered outdoors at Þingvellir for two weeks a year to make laws and settle disputes. The assembly met there for more than eight centuries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Eight of the ten central volcanoes in Vatnajökull National Park lie under ice. When water escapes the glacier’s edge, the sudden flood has an Icelandic name, jökulhlaup.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Icelandic towns have turned heated outdoor pools into gathering places year-round. A soak in a public hot tub can be as much an occasion for conversation as for swimming.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At a Sankirtana performance in Manipur, the audience sits around the performers. Two drummers and a small group of singers and dancers tell stories of Krishna in a hall or courtyard.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The builders of Ramappa Temple in Telangana put porous “floating bricks” high in its tower. Using lighter bricks reduced the weight that the carved stone below had to carry.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: During Navaratri in Gujarat, garba dancers circle an oil lamp inside a perforated earthen pot, or an image of the goddess Amba. The circle moves anticlockwise to singing and clapping.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Papuan noken bag can carry a baby, a catch of fish or a load of firewood. Knotted or woven from plant fibres, it can also be presented as a peace offering.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wayang puppet theatre flourished both in village performances and at the royal courts of Java and Bali. As it spread to other islands, each developed its own music and styles of puppetry.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Prambanan in Java, three temples honour Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, and three others honour the animals that serve them. Scenes from the Ramayana run along the temple walls.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the January feast in Chiapa de Corzo, the word parachicos names both the dancers and the dance they perform in honour of the saints.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the foot of Popocatépetl, houses in Puebla wear tiles on the outside. Their glazed walls are as much part of the historic city as its cathedral.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At El Tajín near the Gulf coast, a pyramid is named for the niches that cover its sides. This city rose to prominence after the fall of Teotihuacan.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Four Quechua-speaking communities rebuild the Q’eswachaka rope bridge over the Apurímac gorge every year. The rebuilding itself is one of the ties between the villages.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On the coast in Ica, Christmas dance groups tell the story of the shepherds and the Wise Men through two complementary traditions, Hatajo de Negritos and Hatajo de Pallitas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Moquegua, Sarawja marks the end of the rainy season and the beginning of harvest. Groups called ruedas, or wheels, dance in circles or parallel rows.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Beqa, Sawau firewalkers trace their gift to an ancestor who went looking for an eel. In the story, the creature he caught could speak and offered him power over fire in return for its freedom.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Fijian drua carries its crew across the ocean on two hulls. The deck between them turns two slender canoe bodies into a platform for long-distance sailing.
options.label: Source

options.text: Fiji’s first colonial capital was Levuka on Ovalau. Its old port still follows the beach in a low line of buildings among mango and coconut trees.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the southern highlands, Huli men grew their own hair to make wigs. An example in Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum is decorated with everlasting flowers.
options.label: Source

options.text: A large Iatmul canoe on the Sepik often has a crocodile for a prow. The carver shapes the head directly at the front of the wooden vessel.
options.label: Source

options.text: Highland farmers at Kuk left their oldest field plans buried in a swamp. Their ditches and planting surfaces show that agriculture developed independently in New Guinea thousands of years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Rennell, what used to be a coral atoll’s lagoon is now Lake Tegano. The whole atoll was lifted above the sea, leaving a lake where seawater once lay.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bamboo supplies whole ensembles in the Solomon Islands. Musicians turn stems into tuned panpipes, so players with different lengths of pipe can carry different parts of a tune.
options.label: Source

options.text: In lagoons off Malaita, families built islands by bringing pieces of reef rock back in canoes. The ground beneath a village could be the accumulated work of generations.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Cook Islands tīvaevae in Te Papa’s collection has a design its maker used for seven wedding quilts. She changed the colours each time she sewed it.
options.label: Source

options.text: A travelling companion of Māori ancestors left a genetic trail across the Pacific. DNA from kiore, the Pacific rat, links early New Zealand populations with lineages in the Cook and Society islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Manihiki, one of the northern atolls, the lagoon serves as a farm. Cultivating oysters for pearls became one of the island’s principal commercial activities.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Yap, stone money can change hands without moving. For the largest carved rings, the community recognises the new owner while the stone stays where it was.
options.label: Source

options.text: Off Pohnpei, people built Nan Madol across a network of artificial islets. Basalt walls still mark the ceremonial compounds, with canoe channels where a town on land might have streets.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the outlying islands of Yap State, the craft of building a sailing canoe is passed on alongside the skill of finding land. Navigators learn to read waves, weather and the night sky.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A CHamoru latte stone comes in two parts. A bowl-shaped cap rests on a stone pillar, and rows of these supports once held buildings above the ground.
options.label: Source

options.text: When an introduced snake wiped out most of Guam’s forest birds, trees lost their seed couriers. Researchers found native seeds no longer reaching damaged forest from intact stands as they did on neighbouring islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: CHamoru sailors built outrigger canoes so fast that European visitors nicknamed them “flying proas.” A large seagoing form is known on Guam as a sakman.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Pentecost Island, the yam harvest is marked by land diving. Participants leap from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles.
options.label: Source

options.text: Oral traditions about Chief Roi Mata tie together three islands. Archaeologists found physical evidence at sites remembered as his home, the place he died and his burial ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A drawing in sand can cross a language boundary in Vanuatu. Communities speaking dozens of languages have shared a way of tracing patterns to communicate and pass on stories.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Taputapuātea on Raiatea, sacred gathering grounds face a lagoon and a passage through the reef. The site connected Polynesian communities whose visitors had to cross the ocean to meet.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Fakarava, thousands of camouflage groupers gather in a reef pass to spawn around the full moon. For a brief window, divers can see fish normally spread across the reef packed together.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 1769 James Cook watched Venus cross the face of the Sun from Tahiti. His drawing records the planet as a little black disc against the bright Sun.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Among Palau’s Rock Islands are lakes of seawater cut off from the open ocean. Some have developed their own distinctive jellyfish populations.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Palauan bai is a meeting house that can also be read. Painted scenes on its timbers preserve stories for the people gathering beneath them.
options.label: Source

options.text: Palauan chiefs could declare a bul, closing an area to harvesting so it could recover. That customary practice helped shape the islands’ system of protected waters.
options.label: Source

options.text: Kiribati once had different calendar dates at opposite ends of the country. In 1995 it changed how its islands reckoned the date so they could share the same working day.
options.label: Source

options.text: The eight islands of the Phoenix group give only a hint of the landscape below. The protected waters around them also contain great seamounts that never break the surface.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Traditional armour from Kiribati used materials an atoll could supply. A shirt of thick coconut fibre could be worn with a helmet made from the spiny skin of a porcupinefish.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Marshallese navigation chart records something a coastline map leaves out. Curved sticks show how ocean swells bend and cross around islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 1946 a fleet of more than seventy ships lay anchored at Bikini Atoll as targets for a nuclear test. The lagoon became a graveyard for part of that fleet.
options.label: Source

options.text: To make a ceremonial dress mat called a jaki-ed, weavers boil and dry a particular kind of pandanus leaf. Beating it releases fibres fine enough to weave into clothing.
options.label: Source

options.text: Mining the phosphate from Nauru’s interior uncovered a forest of sharp limestone pinnacles. Much of the plateau was left too rugged for homes or farming.
options.label: Source

options.text: Nauruans have a tradition of catching and taming frigatebirds. These ocean-going birds, known locally as itsi, have a place in island life beyond their visits to the coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Nauruan flag is a miniature map. The line marks the equator, the star sits south of it like the island, and its twelve points recall the traditional tribes.
options.label: Source

options.text: Before dawn, a kagu can announce itself with a bark. This grey, ground-dwelling bird lives wild only in New Caledonia.
options.label: Source

options.text: New Caledonian crows make tools with hooks. Researchers watched wild birds fashion hooked implements and use them to reach food they could not grasp with their beaks.
options.label: Source

options.text: New Caledonia’s barrier reefs enclose lagoons with room for dugongs. These plant-eating relatives of manatees live alongside turtles and whales in the reef system.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Niue gets rain but has no permanent rivers running across its surface. Water drains through the porous coral limestone that makes up the island.
options.label: Source

options.text: Niuean hiapo is cloth made from bark. Nineteenth-century artists drew fine designs on it freehand, turning the pale surface into an intricate patterned sheet.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Niuean fisher could head out in a small vaka with an outrigger for stability. A common form carries just one or two people along the coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Samoan fine mat can feel almost like silk. Weavers split pandanus leaves into exceptionally narrow strips, and the completed mat can be exchanged at major family occasions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A traditional Samoan tattooist works with a kit of comb-like tools. A second tool taps the pigment-bearing teeth into the skin to build the pattern.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Samoan fale can be a home, kitchen or meeting place. In an open-sided fale, the posts carry the roof and the breeze can pass right through the building.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Tuvalu’s coral atolls, growers raise pulaka, a giant swamp taro, down in dug pits. The gardens bring its roots close to freshwater beneath the island surface.
options.label: Source

options.text: Tuvalu’s game of te ano is played with two balls. The hard balls are traditionally made from pandanus leaves.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the 1890s an expedition brought drilling equipment to Funafuti to test how coral atolls form. The layers beneath the island offered a way to investigate a question Darwin had raised.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Tinian, the House of Taga is marked by immense latte stones. The pillars and caps survive as foundations for a building whose wooden superstructure has gone.
options.label: Source

options.text: The three islets of Maug are pieces of one volcanic rim. Sail between them and the water below you fills an ancient caldera.
options.label: Source

options.text: Carolinian master navigators helped keep long-distance canoe voyaging alive in the Northern Marianas after Spanish colonisation disrupted CHamoru seafaring.
options.label: Source

options.text: Tonga’s 2022 Hunga eruption sent a pressure wave ringing around Earth. Instruments continued to register its passage as it circled the globe over several days.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The Haʻamonga ʻa Maui on Tongatapu looks like a giant stone doorway. Its two upright posts and crosspiece are all slabs of coral limestone.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Tongan lakalaka is a speech you can watch. Performers stand in rows, singing and clapping while their movements deliver meaning alongside the words.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Three customary kingdoms share this one French territory. ʻUvea occupies Wallis, while Alo and Sigave divide Futuna.
options.label: Source

options.text: Wallis has lakes but no surface river network. Rain filters into the ground, while old volcanic craters such as Lalolalo hold pools of standing water.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Wallis and Futuna, makers beat the inner bark of the paper mulberry into sheets of tapa. It becomes a cloth that can be painted without weaving a single thread.
options.label: Source

options.text: Traditional Hawaiian fishponds have a gate called a mākāhā. Water and small fish can pass between its slats, while larger fish stay in the pond.
options.label: Source

options.text: The mark between the last two vowels in Hawaiʻi is a consonant. Called the ʻokina, it signals a glottal stop. A line over a vowel, the kahakō, changes how long the vowel is held.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Hawaiian chain records the motion of an ocean plate. Volcanoes grow over a hot spot and are carried northwest, so islands farther along the chain are generally older.
options.label: Source

options.text: Bagana builds its cone with thick lava that creeps down its flanks. Eruptions have been recorded on this Bougainville volcano since the nineteenth century.
options.label: Source

options.text: One variety of Rotokas, spoken on Bougainville, distinguishes just six consonant sounds. It is one of the smallest consonant inventories linguists have described.
options.label: Source

options.text: In bamboo bands on Bougainville and nearby Buka, players strike tuned tubes with rubber cut from footwear. A worn sandal can find a second life as a musical instrument.
